hints: Look at the two curves in Fig. 10.1 between 07.00 and 08.00. What happens to the solid line first, and what follows a little later on the dashed line?

Pick out peak values with units to prove the link - for example glucose rises from about $4.3 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ to about $6.2 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ while insulin rises from about $30 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$ to about $280 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$.
Think about cause and effect in homeostasis - high glucose is the stimulus detected by the pancreas, insulin is the response that lowers glucose by promoting uptake and glycogenesis.
walkthrough:
See the Pattern in the Graph**
Both curves rise together after the meal at 07.00 and then fall together. Glucose goes up first as it is absorbed from the gut, from about $4.3 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ to a peak of about $6.2 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ at 08.00. Insulin follows, shooting up from a very low level of about $30 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$ to about $280 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$ at the same time. That matching rise and fall is a positive correlation.

Link Stimulus to Response**
A rise in blood glucose is detected by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. They respond by secreting insulin into the blood. So glucose is the trigger and insulin release is the effect.

Explain the Fall Back to Normal**
Insulin makes liver and muscle cells more permeable to glucose and stimulates glycogenesis, the conversion of glucose to glycogen, plus increased respiration. This removes glucose from the blood, so glucose falls back to about $4.4 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ by 09.00. As glucose falls, insulin secretion falls. This is negative feedback restoring the set point.

Final answer: As blood glucose concentration increases, blood insulin concentration increases. E.g. glucose rises from $4.3 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ at 07.00 to $6.2 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ at 08.00, insulin rises from $30 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$ to $280 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$. Increased glucose stimulates insulin release from the pancreas, insulin promotes glucose uptake and conversion to glycogen, returning glucose to the set point by negative feedback.

hints: Compare eating free glucose with eating starch - which one can be absorbed directly across the gut wall and which one needs extra work first?
Recall which enzymes act on starch in the mouth and small intestine and what the final small product must be before absorption.
If glucose enters the blood more slowly, think about how that changes the height of the peak, the timing of the peak, and the size of the insulin response that follows.
walkthrough:
Why Starch Is Slower**
Glucose from a glucose-rich meal needs no digestion and is absorbed quickly. Starch is a large polysaccharide and cannot be absorbed. It must be broken down first by salivary and pancreatic amylase to maltose, then by maltase on the ileum lining to glucose. That hydrolysis takes time.

Effect on the Glucose Curve**
Because glucose is released and absorbed gradually, blood glucose would start to rise later than in Fig. 10.1. The peak would be lower than $6.2 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ because glucose is arriving slowly while body cells are already removing it. The curve would also stay raised for longer and fall more gradually.

Effect on the Insulin Curve**
Insulin secretion follows the glucose stimulus. With a smaller, slower glucose rise, less insulin is released, so the insulin peak would be lower than $280 \text{ pmol dm}^{-3}$ and delayed. Both curves show the same flattened, stretched-out shape.

Final answer: Both glucose and insulin curves would rise after a longer delay, reach lower peaks and fall more slowly / over a longer time. Starch must first be hydrolysed by amylase and maltase to glucose before absorption, so glucose enters blood more slowly.

hints: Glucagon is a first messenger that stays outside the cell. What membrane-bound enzyme is typically activated inside by a G-protein to make a small diffusible signal?
That small molecule made from ATP is called cyclic AMP. Think about its role as a second messenger inside the liver cell.
Second messengers often switch on protein kinases. What is the advantage of one kinase activating many enzymes in a chain?
Finish the story by linking the cascade to glycogen and glucose - what process breaks down glycogen and how does that help blood glucose return to normal?
walkthrough:
From Receptor to Second Messenger**
Glucagon cannot enter the liver cell, so the signal must be carried inside. The activated G-protein activates the enzyme adenylyl cyclase in the cell surface membrane. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP, known as cAMP. cAMP is the second messenger - glucagon was the first.

Cascade and Amplification**
cAMP activates protein kinase. That kinase activates other enzymes, which activate still more enzymes in an enzyme cascade. A common mistake is to think one glucagon makes one glucose. In reality each step activates many molecules of the next enzyme, so the signal is hugely amplified. A tiny amount of glucagon can mobilise a lot of glucose quickly.

Restoring Blood Glucose**
The final enzymes catalyse glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, and also stimulate gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol. Glucose is then released from liver cells into the blood, raising blood glucose concentration back up toward the set point.

Final answer: Activated G-protein activates adenylyl cyclase, which forms cyclic AMP (cAMP) from ATP. cAMP acts as second messenger and activates protein kinase, triggering an enzyme cascade. This amplifies the signal, activating glycogenolysis (and gluconeogenesis) to release glucose into the blood.
